grounded_facts: Sheldon orders pineapple juice instead of his usual orange juice, signaling a change in mood or self-expression.
memories.memory_text: I saw Sheldon order pineapple juice instead of his usual orange juice, and when Sandy questioned him, he said he was feeling 'feisty'—it struck me as a clear shift in his mood.

grounded_facts: Sheldon expresses intent to report Parade of Hope to authorities due to being threatened, but is warned by Burke about severe consequences.
Sheldon speaks with Burke about the threat from Parade of Hope.

memories.memory_text: I was on the phone with Sheldon when he told me he was going to report Parade of Hope after being threatened, and I warned him that if he ratted on them, he’d be lucky if they found his toenails — these guys are the roughest of all the charities.

grounded_facts: Spinner enthusiastically greets Sheldon with a bear hug upon seeing him again.

grounded_facts: Sheldon announces his decision to proceed with the ice show after careful consideration.
memories.memory_text: I remember Sheldon telling me, after giving it a lot of thought, that he'd decided to do the ice show.

grounded_facts: Sheldon declares that the ice show will exclude all sponsors and vendors to maintain purity.
memories.memory_text: I was told by Sheldon that he'd run the ice show himself—no sponsors, no vendors, no crooks—and that not one dirty hand would touch it.

grounded_facts: Sheldon announces that all ticket profits will go toward building a high-quality methadone clinic in Coney Island.
memories.memory_text: I heard from Sheldon that all profits from ticket sales would go toward building a state-of-the-art methadone clinic in Coney Island.

grounded_facts: A dinner gathering where Sheldon and Burke discuss the future of the ice show, interrupted by Spinner's return.
memories.memory_text: I was having dinner with Sheldon, discussing his ice show plans, when Spinner came back and interrupted us; I told Sheldon he couldn't cut out the vendors and the Parade of Hope without risking everything.

grounded_facts: Sheldon declares that he will use his influence to reshape the business rather than be used by it.
memories.memory_text: I recall Sheldon saying he was done letting the business use him, and that it was time he started using the business, with his clout back and not gonna waste it.

grounded_facts: Tommy asks Sheldon to give Spinner a different role in the show to stop the constant cowbell noise.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Tommy asked Sheldon to give Spinner a different role in the show so the cowbell noise would stop, saying it was giving him a headache from morning till night.

grounded_facts: A private conversation between Stokes and Burke while walking in Central Park, discussing business pressures and a potential new deal.
memories.memory_text: I was walking with Stokes through Central Park on a chilly, grey afternoon, talking about business pressures and a possible new deal.

grounded_facts: Stokes physically stops and grabs Burke's arm to emphasize his offer of partnership, appealing to their shared history.
memories.memory_text: I remember Stokes suddenly stopping and grabbing my arm to make his point more forcefully during our walk.

grounded_facts: Stokes offers Burke a partnership on the Takashi deal, suggesting they split profits and return to their previous successful collaboration.
memories.memory_text: Stokes told me he wanted to bring me in as his partner on the Takashi deal, splitting profits fifty-fifty and getting back to how things used to be between us.

grounded_facts: Burke responds to Stokes's offer by noting the dangerous nature of the proposed path forward.
memories.memory_text: I told Stokes this was very sticky ground we were about to walk on, letting him know I saw the risks in what he was proposing.

grounded_facts: Burke arrives at the alley and interrupts the ongoing confrontation between Merv and Johnny, shifting the focus of the scene.
memories.memory_text: I arrived at the alley and stepped in, interrupting the confrontation between Merv and Johnny, shifting the focus to me.

grounded_facts: Burke approaches Merv with a casual but pointed greeting, suggesting familiarity and underlying tension.
memories.memory_text: I approached Merv and said, 'Merv Green. How's tricks, kid?' knowing our history carried some tension beneath the casual tone.

grounded_facts: Burke suggests to Merv that Mopes may be cooperating with authorities or speaking to people who could threaten their business, possibly wearing a wire.
Burke informs Merv that Mopes may be cooperating with outsiders and could be wearing a wire, implying betrayal.
memories.memory_text: I told Merv I think Mopes might be talking to people he shouldn't, and I wouldn't be surprised if he's wearing a wire.

grounded_facts: Burke ends the conversation with Merv by hailing a cab and leaving for another engagement across town.
Burke cuts short the discussion by claiming another appointment and leaving in a cab.
memories.memory_text: I ended the conversation with Merv because I had another appointment across town; I looked at my watch, said I needed to go, hailed a cab, and left.

grounded_facts: Stokes voices anxiety about the escalating situation and doubts about involving Buggy.
memories.memory_text: I saw Stokes shakily sipping his drink and later burying his head in his hands, clearly anxious about getting Buggy involved.

grounded_facts: A clandestine meeting between Burke, Stokes, and Buggy Ding-Dong in a nightclub to discuss and act on their criminal predicament.
memories.memory_text: I sat with Stokes in a booth, called Buggy to join us, and told him it was time to put this thing to rest because I knew we had to act now.

grounded_facts: Burke gives Buggy an envelope, signaling payment for a task related to resolving their ongoing crisis.
Burke formally engages Buggy for a dangerous task, referencing a metaphor about the rhino being up past bedtime, implying violence.
memories.memory_text: I handed Buggy the envelope with the money and told him it was time to put this thing to rest — the rhino's up past his bedtime, after all.

grounded_facts: Smoochy is crowned and left alone in a symbolic new world during the performance.
memories.memory_text: I saw Smoochy being brought to a room with a gleaming white desk, sitting behind it as the fairy princess placed a crown on his head and floated away, leaving him alone in what seemed like a new world where he sat proudly.

grounded_facts: A theatrical ice-skating opera depicting Smoochy's life, unfolding at Madison Square Garden.
memories.memory_text: I was at Madison Square Garden watching a theatrical ice-skating opera about Smoochy's life, and I could tell things were getting tense.

grounded_facts: Buggy fires a shot from the catwalk, wounding a Rhinette but not disrupting the performance.
memories.memory_text: I inferred that Buggy must have fired a shot from the catwalk and wounded a Rhinette, but the gunshot was muffled by the music and no one noticed.

grounded_facts: Randolph shouts to warn Sheldon of danger, though initially unheard.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed Randolph shouting toward Sheldon and running around the rink's edge, trying to get his attention, though Sheldon didn't seem to hear him at first.

grounded_facts: Tommy and her crew notice Randolph being chased and begin pursuing him.
memories.memory_text: I saw the commotion in the audience and noticed Randolph running through the crowd toward the stairwell, so I started pursuing him with Tommy and the crew.

grounded_facts: Randolph pushes past security and reaches the rink to warn Sheldon.
memories.memory_text: I saw Randolph push past security and run toward the rink, and I noticed him making his way through the crowd as Stokes and I watched from our position.

grounded_facts: Smoochy finds and cradles the fallen 'Moochy' during a symbolic reenactment.
memories.memory_text: I saw Smoochy find and cradle the fallen 'Moochy' during the symbolic reenactment in Chinatown.

grounded_facts: Nora verbally accuses Burke of selling out Sheldon after seeing the rifle.
memories.memory_text: Nora yelled at me that I sold Sheldon out and called me a snake after she saw the rifle.

grounded_facts: Stokes tries to calm Nora by claiming he is grooming her for leadership.
memories.memory_text: I heard Stokes tell Nora he was grooming her for leadership when she confronted us.

grounded_facts: Nora realizes Stokes and Burke are complicit, confronts them, and physically attacks Burke.
memories.memory_text: I tried to stop Nora from climbing out of the box, but she spun around and punched me before running off.

grounded_facts: After Nora's outburst and the growing chaos, Stokes and Burke flee in opposite directions.
memories.memory_text: After Nora punched me and ran for the rink, Stokes asked me what we should do, and I shouted 'Survival of the fittest!' before I ran off through the panicked crowd, leaving him behind.

grounded_facts: Nora screams a warning to Sheldon just before the final shot.
memories.memory_text: I stopped Nora from climbing out of the box when she screamed a warning to Sheldon.

grounded_facts: Buggy takes aim and fires, but Randolph tackles him mid-shot, causing the bullet to miss Sheldon's head.
memories.memory_text: I saw Buggy take aim and fire, but Randolph tackled him mid-shot, causing the bullet to miss Sheldon's head.

grounded_facts: Buggy shoots at approaching cops during struggle on catwalk.
memories.memory_text: I saw Buggy raise his rifle and shoot at the cops during the struggle on the catwalk.

grounded_facts: After a struggle on the catwalk, Buggy loses grip and plummets to his death.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed Buggy lose his grip during the struggle and fall from the catwalk after clinging to Randolph's leg, desperately grabbing at his foot before slipping off and plummeting to his death.

grounded_facts: Nora informs Sheldon that Burke has been working with Stokes, urging him to act.
memories.memory_text: I was told that Burke's with Stokes, that he's been in it all along.

grounded_facts: After learning of Burke's betrayal, Sheldon pulls out his gun and runs toward the exit to confront Burke.
memories.memory_text: I realized Sheldon must have found out about my betrayal and came after me with his gun.

grounded_facts: Burke pushes through the crowd at the exit to escape, noticing Sheldon chasing him.
memories.memory_text: I saw Sheldon chasing me, so I pushed through the crowd at the exit and forced my way out to escape.

grounded_facts: Burke runs away from Madison Square Garden down 33rd Street to escape pursuit.
memories.memory_text: I ran away from Madison Square Garden down 33rd Street to escape whoever was after me.

grounded_facts: Sheldon, still in skates and wearing the damaged Smoochy head, chases Burke after spotting him from a distance.
memories.memory_text: I looked behind me and saw the disfigured Smoochy—still on skates—chasing after me, and I realized it was Sheldon.

grounded_facts: Burke sees the approaching figure of the damaged Smoochy and quickly turns a street corner to avoid capture.
memories.memory_text: I looked behind me and saw the nightmarish, disfigured Smoochy chasing after me, so I quickly turned the corner to get away.

grounded_facts: Burke expresses anger and betrayal that Sheldon pointed a gun at him — a gun he had given as a gift.
memories.memory_text: I remember jumping out and knocking Sheldon down, then getting on top of him and strangling him — he had the nerve to point a gun at me, a gun I gave him as a gift, and I shouted at him about how disrespectful that was.

grounded_facts: Nora intervenes in the fight between Sheldon and Burke by shooting a gun to stop Burke from strangling Sheldon.
Nora points a gun at Burke and threatens to shoot unless he stops strangling Sheldon.
memories.memory_text: I was strangling Sheldon when I heard a gunshot and looked up to see Nora pointing his gun at me, telling me to let him go—she threatened to shoot me if I didn't stop.

grounded_facts: Burke confirms his responsibility for the murder of Spinner, framing it as a regrettable but acceptable loss.
memories.memory_text: I told Sheldon that Spinner's death was a tragic mistake, but really, one less mick in the world isn't such a loss — and I couldn't help but laugh at how it all played out.

grounded_facts: Sheldon publicly discards his Smoochy costume and declares that he is no longer pretending to be the character.
memories.memory_text: I saw Sheldon tear off his Smoochy costume and step out of it, then he looked at me and said, 'I'm not Smoochy.'

grounded_facts: Tommy convinces Sheldon not to kill Burke by appealing to his role as Smoochy and his importance to children.
memories.memory_text: I heard Tommy arrive and tell Sheldon not to do it, reminding him of who he is as Smoochy and how important he is to the kids, and I watched as he handed over the gun and broke down, realizing I was spared because of what she said.

grounded_facts: Sheldon, after pointing a gun at Burke's head and preparing to shoot, is persuaded by Tommy to hand over the gun and spare Burke's life.
memories.memory_text: I saw Sheldon shaking as he pointed the gun at my head, and I could tell he was struggling to pull the trigger—I felt petrified as he stood there with his eyes closed, deciding my fate.

grounded_facts: A violent and emotionally charged confrontation between Sheldon, Burke, and Nora, culminating in a moral decision about vengeance and identity.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed the whole violent struggle with Sheldon and Nora, from when I ambushed him to when Nora took the gun and pointed it at me, and later when Sheldon held it on me — I saw the fear in both their eyes and realized it had become a moment where he would decide whether to kill me or not.

grounded_facts: Smoochy theatrically calls upon the Magic Cookie Bag, reinforcing the show's ceremonial structure.

grounded_facts: Nora observes the children's joy and for the first time acknowledges Smoochy's genuine impact on them.
memories.memory_text: I saw Nora watching the kids laughing in the bleachers, and for the first time, I realized she could finally see the real connection I have with them as Smoochy.

grounded_facts: The Magic Cookie Bag is lowered from the ceiling and delivered to Smoochy during the show, marking a ritual moment in the taping.

grounded_facts: Randolph mutters a derogatory comment about Smoochy under his breath, expressing contempt.

grounded_facts: Burke pats Sheldon's head like a dog and later gives him an affectionate slap, treating him more like a pet than a peer.
memories.memory_text: Burke patted my head like I was a dog, treating me more like a pet than a person during the meeting.

grounded_facts: Burke belittles Nora’s professional worth by suggesting she would be organizing puppet shows for children without Sheldon.

grounded_facts: Nora counters Burke's claim of Sheldon's indispensability by reminding everyone that she and Stokes resurrected Sheldon's career when no one else would.

grounded_facts: A gathering convened by Sheldon to address perceived miscommunications, which quickly turns into a negotiation and power struggle involving his representation and value.
memories.memory_text: I called the meeting to clear up communication issues, but it quickly turned into a negotiation where my role and value were being contested.

grounded_facts: Burke publicly declares his authority as Sheldon's agent and asserts that Sheldon, as the creator and owner of Smoochy, holds all leverage in negotiations with Stokes and Nora.
memories.memory_text: I saw Burke declare himself as my agent and assert that I own and control every part of Smoochy, positioning me as the one holding all the power in the negotiations.

grounded_facts: Sheldon is celebrated for his new role as star and executive producer of the Smoochy show, granting him creative control, part ownership, merchandising discretion, and a corporate penthouse.

grounded_facts: Spinner Dunn approaches Sheldon with excitement and introduces himself, shaking his hand with overwhelming enthusiasm.

When Frank mentioned Sheldon Mopes, I actually laughed—Smoochy the Rhino? The guy was a joke, stuck doing hospital gigs, and the idea of building a show around him felt like surrender.

I watched Sheldon shove that gross soy dog into his mouth, talking with food flying, and then he yanked Smoochy’s busted head out of a bag like it was some holy relic—screaming about integrity like anyone at Kidnet actually cared.
I ignored Sheldon’s raised hand and kept going with the recap—ice pops yes, string cheese no, shampoo split still up in the air. He wasn’t going to derail this meeting with his sanctimonious act.
After I tossed the Frisbee into the hall and Sheldon went to get it, I told John to shut the door—and then lock it. The click was quiet, but it made the point.

I stopped walking, looked Sheldon in the eye, and told him straight—his being on TV had nothing to do with talent or value, only because Rainbow Randolph was a scumbag; I delivered him like a bag of groceries, and he should stop pretending he mattered more than that.

I told Sheldon the 'Please and Thank You Song' was cut because it's sappy and eats into the 'Cookie Song'—then I ordered him to reinstate the original lyrics, the ones glorifying sugar. He called me out, said I see kids as wallets with pigtails. It stung, but I couldn't show it.
I was ready to roll my eyes at another grotesque puppet routine, but then I saw the kids—real laughter, real joy, their faces lit up like they actually believed in that stupid Magic Cookie Bag.
I told Burke there was no excuse for him, and then I reminded him that we were the ones who dug Sheldon up and handed him his show when no one else would.
I told him 'no' when he asked me to lunch, and then made it clear I wouldn't change my mind — he didn't get to waltz in here acting like we were going to be partners after everything.
He tried to make small talk on his way out, muttering about the plant like it meant something — I didn’t even look up, just let him walk out alone.
I walked in and threw the paper on his desk—'Congratulations on your little ice show'—and watched his face go blank. He had the nerve to look confused after selling out like that.
I saw him standing there in that stupid knit cap and sunglasses, like he could just hide from what he'd done—like I wouldn't recognize the guy who performed in front of a fifty-foot swastika.
He brought up the balcony, that stupid dance—like any of it meant something. I told him I was drunk. It was easier than saying none of it ever mattered.

I remember the way he just walked in like he owned the place, tossing around that smug 'R man is back' crap while I was still reeling from the Smoochy mess. When he put his hands on me and tried to kiss me, I shoved him hard—felt the couch rattle when he nearly went over the table.
I backed him into the wall and asked point-blank if he set Sheldon up. He didn’t answer—just stared at me, then called me a bitch. That’s when I punched him in the jaw. I felt it connect, solid.

I walked into Spinner Dunn's, scanned the room, and asked Tommy and Spinner if Burke had been in—my voice was sharp, impatient, because I needed to find him. When I said it was about Sheldon, Spinner suddenly stopped banging his head and looked up, saying my brother's name like he actually remembered him.

I stood there beside Sheldon as the drumroll echoed, and when he said he wouldn’t be back without me, I finally admitted I was sorry—really sorry—for not believing him, for getting caught up in all that anti-Smoochy noise.

I stood there trying to find the words, my voice quiet but insistent—I just needed to know where we stood, after everything. When I said it was about us, I saw the shift in his face, that flicker of discomfort, and I knew I’d crossed into something raw.

One second I was bracing for another deflection, and the next he was on me—kissing me hard, no warning. I didn’t hesitate; I tore at his costume, pulled him down, and let everything else burn away in that mess on the floor.
I had my arm around Sheldon while he stood there staring at Spinner in the casket, barely holding it together. He kept saying it was his fault, like he could’ve stopped any of it.

I started singing 'The Last Nappy Time' quietly, the one Rickets the Hippo did—sang it because it got me through my mom’s death. Sheldon joined in, and then we just… held each other while the bagpipes played.
I heard Tommy say it wasn't Smiley who killed Spinner — it was Parade of Hope. When he named Merv Green, something in me snapped, like all the lies I’d swallowed finally had a face.
I remember the way Merv Green grabbed me at that 'Feed the Children' benefit—smiling like a saint while his hand squeezed my ass. I knew right then he was a scumbag.
I stood in the warehouse and watched Danny raise the hatchet while Merv begged. I didn’t look away when the screaming stopped.
I was reorganizing the schedule cards when he came up behind me, ripped a Smoochy card off the board, and shoved it in my face, talking about a 'rhino problem' and deals in his culture.

He pulled a switchblade out of nowhere and held it to my throat—cold metal against my skin—then said they'd kill everyone at the network, starting with the pretty ones, before throwing it into a Smoochy card.
I told Sheldon the truth about Stokes trying to replace him with Takashi, that smug international puppet, but before I could make him see how serious it was, everything fell apart.
Randolph burst in yelling about us being together, waving that damn gun, and suddenly I was on the defensive about Jingle Jackson and Johnny—like my past was some punchline he got to expose.
I handed Randolph tea, then asked Sheldon what he thought he was doing with that gun — he just kept loading it like I wasn’t even there.

I was still watching the opera, caught up in the stupid pageantry, when something in the way Stokes and Burke kept glancing at each other made my gut tighten—like they weren’t just nervous, like they *knew* something was coming.
I didn’t see the rifle at first, but once I did—up on the catwalk, Buggy hunched over it—I bolted from the booth, screaming Sheldon’s name, my voice cracking as I ran for the rink stairs.
I finally reached Sheldon through the chaos, smoke stinging my eyes, and grabbed him—told him Burke was with Stokes, that he’d been in it all along.
I shouted 'No, Sheldon, don't!' as he pulled the gun from his costume—my voice cracked, but he didn’t stop, just ran into the smoke after Burke.
I picked up the gun and told Burke to let Sheldon go, or I'd pump one in that Grecian Formula scalp of his.
After the shots rang out from behind us, I saw the fear in Sheldon's eyes, so I told him it was just a bus backfire and patted his back—like I could make it okay.
I called him 'Smoochy' and told him it was time to go home—like it was just another end to a long day, even though everything had changed.
We kissed—really kissed—and I didn’t pull away, even with the music swelling and the world blurring around us. I let it happen.

memories.memory_text: I was dancing through Rainbowland in my yellow bow tie, singing 'Friends Come In All Sizes' with the Krinkle Kids, and every voice rose with mine on that big finish — I could feel the joy blasting out of me like a rainbow cannon.
I took a gulp of my Scotch, opened the briefcase, and saw five grand staring me in the face—cold, crisp bills that meant I could breathe for one more night.

I turned to leave with the briefcase, and suddenly they were screaming at me with guns drawn—'Freeze, you cocksucker!'—then the feds poured in from every direction, surrounding me like I was some kind of animal.

I stood there in the cold dawn light, watching newspapers spill onto the street like garbage, each one screaming my name in those ugly bold headlines—'Rainbow Randolph Busted'—like I was some common criminal.
I stood there watching them roll up the backdrops and haul away the rainbow—my rainbow—while some grunt swept up the glitter like it was just trash.
I shouted in the rain, 'I was Rainbow fucking Randolph!'—my voice cracking as I tried to make Frank see who I used to be, how the world stopped when I walked in.
I grabbed Frank's coat and begged him to get my slot back. When he left, I shouted that the wheels were turning, then muttered to myself about clean men falling into mud.
I stood there on the dock, just me and the river, no one answering, no one listening—again.
They replaced me with that rhino freak because they called me a degenerate scumbag — like I’m nothing, like I didn’t build that show.
I saw Burke walk out after shaking hands with that rhino freak, and when I confronted him, he looked me dead in the eye and called me a cigarette butt—just tossed me aside like I was nothing.
I slipped my homemade cookies into Smoochy’s magic bag and tossed his stupid little treats in the trash—let him choke on what I left behind.
I found my old costume in a box labeled 'Rainbow Randolph crap'—I held it close, smelled it, and heard the kids laughing again… I knew I had to come back.

They grabbed me, those three brutes in uniform, and just started dragging me down the stairs—kicking, punching, throwing me around like I was nothing. I remember the cold metal of the door hitting my back right before they hurled me out.

I remember the headline—'Rainbow Randolph Interrupts Smoochy Taping'—and those words burned into my eyes, reducing me to a joke, a punchline about penises while that rhino sits there, patted like a pet.
I kicked the door open and tackled Angelo—he was supposed to be loyal, a Krinkle Kid like me, not some rhino groupie.
After he punched me and put a gun to my face, I started crying—I just wanted to know if I could stay, I had nowhere else.

I showed Angelo the bump on my eye and pulled back my lip to show him the gap where my tooth used to be—told him network security did that when I went back to the studio. I spat the bay leaf on the floor and drank straight from the gin bottle, telling him what they sowed, they’d reap—I meant every word.
I asked Sheldon if he took glee in stealing Rainbow Randolph's time slot and shoveling dirt on his corpse, pushing him to admit he hated the man.
I snapped at Sheldon, yelling that Rainbow Randolph was a fucking asshole and demanding he admit he hated him—only to be met with silence and discomfort when he changed the subject to the radio.

I walked into Nora's place, threw off my jacket, and told her the R man was back—ready to whistle happy tunes for the little chillens, starting Monday. I flopped down on her couch like I owned the place, demanding a Scotch like nothing had changed.

She got in my face, accusing me of setting up Sheldon, backing me against the wall—her eyes locked on mine like a cop. I didn't answer, just threw back that she was always a bitch with accusations, and then—bam—the next thing I felt was her fist cracking my jaw.
I stood there with my lawyer, bloodied but still proud, and told those reporters to their faces — being hated in this country is a badge of honor, not a shame.
An egg hit me right in the face — cold, slimy — and I couldn't hold it back, I just shouted it was unfair, that it was mean, I was on the verge of tears.

I was just sitting there, cheese curls in my lap, and then I saw him—Smoochy—on the screen, grinning like some horned saint while everyone cheered. The pressure in my head built until I couldn't think, just feel the rage burning behind my eyes.

After I kicked the TV and swung the lamp, Angelo came running, took it from me, and then pointed at the door—told me to get out. I barely got out 'Where am I supposed to go?' before he said he didn't care.

I saw that guy with his stupid rhino picture and pamphlets, and when he asked me to donate, something snapped—I jumped over the table and grabbed him, screaming that I'm the one who needs saving, that I'm broke and homeless and a peanut shell in the shape of a man.
After screaming at that guy, I grabbed the metal donation can off his table and ran, yelling 'Save the Rainbow!' over and over, my slippers slapping the pavement as I fled.

I stood on that table in Times Square, raised the gasoline can high, and shouted to the crowd about the injustice Smoochy brought on me—then I poured it all over myself, the cold shock of it soaking through my clothes, clinging to my skin.
After I soaked myself, I held up the pack of matches for everyone to see—my hand steady despite the fear, a final warning meant for Smoochy’s eyes alone, a fire waiting to happen if he didn’t show.
I finally got the match lit, held it up like a torch for the world to see — and then this little girl just walks up and blows it out, smiling like it was a birthday candle.

I was still standing there, the match gone, the girl vanished — and then the limo roared past me, the crowd screaming for Smoochy like I wasn't even there. I dropped to my knees and screamed into the sky, but no one looked back.

I was begging Angelo on the pay phone in Times Square, telling him I didn't do it, that I was soaked in gasoline and people thought I was crazy, but he still wouldn't let me come back—he said I had to go underground.
I told Angelo it was time to heal, to accept that Smoochy had won and that I’d move forward with faith—justice would prevail, I said, even though I’m wanted for a murder I didn’t commit.
I saw them in the newspaper—Sheldon and Nora, arms around each other at Spinner’s wake—and something inside me snapped. I screamed so loud the birds flew from the rafters.
I was lounging on Sheldon's sofa, fresh out of the shower in his robe, eating grapes and flipping through National Geographic when the phone rang—I picked it up singing, not a care in the world.

When Angelo said Buggy Double D was working for Burke Bennett, something snapped—I felt it in my gut. I tore the towel off my head and knew I had to get to the Garden, cops or not. I have to warn the rhino.

Don't do this to me, Frank. I'm in deep, deep shit. They kicked me out of the corporate penthouse... I got bookies breathing down my neck. I'm homeless! Don't you hear what I'm saying? I'm not gonna make it! The clock's ticking! Put yourself in my shoes, for Christ's sake!

memories.memory_text: I was carrying Smoochy’s body over my shoulder and his head in a bag when she introduced herself—then I saw her card said 'Nora Bishop. V.P. of Development. Kidnet.' I remember thinking, Good gravy. You work for Kidnet? before shaking her hand too hard, too fast.
I tried to tell Nora how much I’ve contributed—the two thousand songs, the messages behind them—hoping she’d see me as more than just a costume, but she didn’t even pretend to care.
When she stopped and looked at me, I thought maybe she’d finally listen—instead, she said I was just a delivery, like groceries, and that my only job was to smile and nod.
I held that crumpled show rundown and asked Nora why they cut the 'Please and Thank You Song'—how could they remove the one part that actually taught the kids something?
I turned back and told her, 'When I go out there I see kids. You see wallets with pigtails'—the words just came out, but I knew they cut deeper than any contract.
I couldn't believe it—creative control, part ownership, a dressing room with a toilet. I kept asking myself if I was dreaming, it felt too good to be real.
He handed me a gun in a paper bag, and when I pulled it out, I flinched—I just dropped it. I told him I'd never touched a gun, that I don't believe in them.

I saw my face on the cover of Variety, smiling back at me under the headline that said I was starting today as executive producer — then I paid for the magazine, looked up at the Kidnet building, and walked inside, breathing deep like I was stepping into something real.

I remember the heavy thud of the wad of cash hitting my desk, how Ben just dropped it there like it was nothing—like my integrity was for sale. I picked it up and threw it back at him, told him I’d make an exception to take the trash out early.
I tore the contract in half right there at the table—felt the paper split in my hands—and told Burke that Smoochy doesn't sell out, not like those guys who paint driveways black and call it paving.
I told Spinner his performance was great, but I had to mention his elbow—he nearly knocked out Pinky’s tooth.
When Nora called Spinner a mental patient, I snapped—I had to defend him. He’s not broken, he’s just gentle, with a sweet innocent brain like a five-year-old.

I was just trying to hail a cab after leaving the Kidnet building when a man in a suit smiled and told me to get in the limo—he seemed friendly at first, but then he showed me a gun and called me 'rhino' like it was some kind of joke.

Merv Green sat across from me in the limo, smiling like this was some kind of business meeting, and told me Smoochy was starting tomorrow — benefits, banquets, all of it — like I had any choice in the matter.

I remember the door suddenly popping open, and then being shoved out into the street — just tossed like garbage — while the limo idled at the curb, Merv’s voice still hanging in the air about ice skates.

I remember doing the Klunky-Wunky dance with Nora, laughing at how ridiculous it was, and then suddenly kissing her—really kissing her—after years of feeling like no one truly got why Smoochy mattered.
Right after Nora left, the phone rang—some call I had to take, I guess, though I just wanted to stay in that moment, still tasting orange juice and wondering if any of it really happened.

I stepped up to the mic, heart pounding, staring at that massive swastika behind me while hundreds of Nazis chanted my name—'Heil Smoochy!'—and I could barely breathe. All I managed to say was, 'It's my sincere hope that I'm dreaming right now... what's the deal with the swastikas?'

One second I was standing there, frozen, trying to make sense of the nightmare, and then suddenly cops stormed in, yelling, and chaos exploded all around me. I didn't move—I just stayed in the middle, completely unsure what to do as Nazis scattered like roaches.

I was in handcuffs, flashing lights all around, and reporters shouting—asking if I was part of the Aryan Brotherhood, if I admired Hitler. I kept saying it was a mix-up, that I didn’t hate anyone, but they twisted my words.
I was cut off mid-sentence, trying to explain, and then suddenly shoved into the back of a squad car—the door slammed, the sirens started, and we sped off before I could say anything more.

I remember sitting in that precinct chair, hands pressed into cold ink, staring ahead as the camera flashed—then suddenly I was back in the studio, Smoochy spinning with a child in his arms, laughing, the jungle set bright and alive… and then it was gone.

There was no sound, no heat—just the costume hanging in black space, flames curling around the fur, the colors melting into ash. I couldn’t move. I just watched it burn, like it was me inside that suit.
I stood there in my knit cap and sunglasses, heart pounding, begging Nora to believe me when I said I didn’t know it was a Nazi rally—she just kept walking, like my words didn’t even matter.
